extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism/media studies; journalists and media theorists interested in news production
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria and concepts used to analyze how news is produced, framed, and legitimized — focusing on institutional routines, sourcing, framing/typification, and the ideological effects of news work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of news / newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Defining what counts as newsworthy is historically derived and embedded in contemporary understandings of significance, institutional behavior, and motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess news selections against the cultural and historical rules available to newsworkers: which events are framed as interesting or important at a given historical moment. Example: 1920s professional definitions drew on contemporary notions of science and distrust of public opinion. Verbosity: newsworthiness is not innate but produced by available cultural resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embeddedness in legitimated institutions and centralized news gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Newswork is wed to legitimated social institutions; centralized beats, bureaus, wire services and networks become objectified as the appropriate sites for information gathering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether coverage privileges institutional sources and whether organizational structures (beats/bureaus/wires) determine what is treated as legitimate news. Example: dispersion of reporters to institutional beats creates a 'news net' centered on legitimated institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectification of sources, sites, and processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites of news gathering and the processes of news production are treated as objective, taken-for-granted locations and methods for producing facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for routines or statements that present particular institutions (e.g., 'the city', 'the state') or processes (deadlines, beats) as natural or unquestioned sources of truth. This includes the transformation of reporting practices into 'normal' procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typification and re-typification (categorization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworkers apply typifications—classifying occurrences according to prior models of how events unfold—and revise those typifications when events deviate from expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how events are initially classified (spot news, continuing story, scandal, etc.) and how classifications change over time. Examples: Watergate cast successively as break-in, investigation, scandal, legislative inquiry, resignation. Typification both generates and limits newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorizing through juxtaposition and categorization
rubrics_metrics.description: By juxtaposing facts and grouping diverse phenomena under single categories (e.g., 'unrest'), news creates and claims theoretical relationships among events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the arrangement of items implies causal or categorical links that constitute a theory (implicit or explicit). Example: grouping strikes, short work hours, and a jailed conspiracy case under 'unrest' implies a common interpretive frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexicality and reflexivity of news
rubrics_metrics.description: News is indexical (grounded in local, pretheoretic formulations) and reflexive (both describing and participating in social life); it draws on and feeds back into everyday understandings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for practices where news relies on actors' pretheoretic understandings (e.g., reporters' reliance on committee chairs' predictions) and for instances where news changes the social meanings it reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on pretheoretic formulations of sources and official statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: News (and social science) frequently uses data and accounts produced by actors who were not operating with the researcher's definitions (e.g., coroners, police), so findings reflect those pretheoretic categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize whether categories used in reporting (or datasets quoted) reflect the original actors' understandings rather than analytically precise definitions. Example: Durkheim's use of official suicide statistics conflates classificatory practices with theoretical variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to professionalism and veridical representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic professionalism is often presented as analogous to scientific objectivity and as a claim to present veridical accounts of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze rhetorical appeals to 'science', neutrality, or First Amendment traditions that are used to legitimate coverage. Note how such claims can function as resources to protect professional status or to mask institutional interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naive empiricism: transforming information into 'objective facts'
rubrics_metrics.description: Through unreflective methods, newswork turns information derived from sources and routines into 'facts' presented as normal, natural, and taken-for-granted descriptions of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify reporting practices that present contested or constructed information as plain facts, without reflexive discussion of methods or source limitations. Consider how this masks the constructed nature of the account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routinization: deadlines, rhythm, and stages of processing
rubrics_metrics.description: News production is routinized by imposed rhythms (deadlines, stages of processing) that structure what can be covered and how events are sequenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how temporal constraints and routine stages (e.g., spot news vs. planned coverage) shape story selection and framing. Example: editors plan reporter availability for predicted continuing stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational chains of command (territorial, institutional, topical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Territorial, institutional, and topical chains of command in news organizations define assignments and priorities, influencing which topics are considered 'institutionally interesting'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how hierarchical structures privilege some beats (political/territorial) over others (women's news, sports), thereby shaping institutional attention and reinforcing status quos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of power in construction of social reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Different actors have unequal resources to impose definitions of situations; newsworkers and certain institutions have disproportionate power to construct and reproduce social meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whose voices are amplified or treated as authoritative and how that distribution of access/resources shapes the constructed reality presented in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and containment of controversy and dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: By selecting sources, framing issues, and institutionalizing beats, news organizations create and control controversy and contain dissent within acceptable channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for practices that limit dissent (e.g., relying on institutional spokespeople, balancing only among official parties) and for mechanisms that routinize how controversy is presented and confined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional practices, sharing/hoarding, and source relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal norms among reporters—sharing or hoarding information, social ties, negotiating coverage—shape who is a 'good' source and how stories are developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the informal social organization of reporters (collaboration, competition, source cultivation) and how these practices influence story content and sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbolic imagery for dramatic impact
rubrics_metrics.description: News uses symbolic images and narratives (photographs, dramatized descriptions) to achieve dramatic effects that can alter public understandings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note how imagery and symbolic framing (e.g., John-John saluting coffin, celebration photos) are used strategically to amplify drama and shape public interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as social resource and reciprocal influence with audience
rubrics_metrics.description: News not only draws on everyday understandings as resources but also serves as a social resource that audiences and movements use to act and make sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how news content becomes a tool for social actors (movements, officials) to disseminate meanings, and how audience uptake feeds back into subsequent news production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological function of procedures — 'interested procedures' as methods of not knowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures embedded in institutions (indexicality, reflexivity, objectification) can operate as 'interested procedures' that conceal rather than reveal, functioning ideologically to truncate possibilities for institutional transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically interrogate routine procedures for whether they reproduce institutional interests or obstruct alternative understandings; look for evidence of self-fulfilling prophecies and unexamined methodological assumptions.
